theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A community development officer in May Pen wants to run an education project on dengue prevention. What should she do first?
options: Print 2,000 leaflets and hand them out at the market
Book the community centre for a Saturday morning
Find out what residents already know, do and need
Ask a popular artiste to record a radio jingle

questions.stem: Which method gives the fullest picture of a community's learning needs?
options: A survey, focus groups and existing local data together
Asking only the community leader what he thinks people need

options: It means the officer does not need to do any planning
It removes the need for a budget
It lets residents take over the funding

options: After the last session, when the results are known
Only if the funder asks for a report
At the planning stage, with a baseline before delivery

questions.stem: A project budgeted J$80,000 for printing but spent J$92,000. What is the overspend as a percentage of the budget?

options: 2 May

options: Topic A

questions.stem: A session will show residents how to make up a mild bleach solution for cleaning water storage containers. What must the facilitator do?
options: Follow the label, wear gloves and never mix it

options: Print all 3,000 and correct any mistakes next year

questions.stem: A district has 1,600 households. The project's home visits reached 1,200 of them. What percentage were reached?

options: Each participant
The venue owner
The project coordinator

questions.stem: An evaluation shows that men aged 20 to 35 hardly attended. What should the next project do?
options: Ask young men when, where and how they would join

options: Promise to keep it a secret and take no further action

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names the process of finding out what a community already knows, does and needs before a project is planned?
Project objectives should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. What one word, made from their first letters, describes them?
What two-word term names a trained member of the community who goes on teaching others in their own group after the project?
A project's six sessions cost J$18,500 each. What is the total cost of the sessions, in J$?
A quiz average rose from 50% before a workshop to 80% after it. By how many percentage points did it rise?
What one-word term names the starting measurement, taken before a project begins, that later results are compared with?
What two-word term names a small, guided group discussion used to explore residents' views on a topic?
A project cost J$360,000 and 225 people took part. What was the cost per participant, in J$?
What one word names a person's free agreement, after being told what it involves, to take part or to be photographed?
What one word names the checks made on volunteers who will work with children, such as references and a police record check?
What one word names a project's ability to keep its benefits going after the funding and the project team have gone?
Of 80 residents registered, 68 completed the course. What is the completion rate, as a percentage?
What three-letter short form names a non-profit group run by and for local residents, such as a citizens' association or youth club?
A project of eight weekly sessions starts in week 3 of the plan. In which week of the plan is the last session?
What two-word term names the statement of what a participant will be able to do by the end of a session?

essays.stem: Explain how you would carry out a needs assessment before planning a community education project on solid waste and illegal dumping in a Spanish Town community.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first gather existing information: complaints to the municipal corporation, collection schedules, photos of dumping sites and any health data on rats or mosquitoes. I would then meet community leaders, the citizens' association, churches and schools to explain the purpose and ask for their help. To hear residents directly, I would run a short survey of a sample of households, chosen street by street so all areas are included, asking how they dispose of waste, what they know about collection days and what stops them using proper methods. I would hold two or three focus groups, for example with young men, vendors and elderly residents, because their reasons may differ. A walk-through with residents would map the worst sites. I would then analyse the results to separate knowledge gaps, such as not knowing collection days, from problems education cannot fix, such as missed collections, which I would refer to the authorities. The findings would be shared back with the community and used to set priorities, objectives and a baseline for measuring later change.
markingPoints: Uses existing data and records
Consults leaders and community groups
Uses a fair survey and focus groups with different groups
Analyses results, separating learning needs from other problems
Shares findings and uses them to set priorities and a baseline

essays.stem: Prepare an outline plan for a six-week financial literacy project for young adults aged 18 to 25 in a Montego Bay community, covering aims, objectives, content, methods, resources and evaluation.
essays.modelAnswer: The aim is to help young adults manage money and avoid harmful debt. Objectives: by the end of week six, 40 participants will have a written monthly budget, 30 will have opened or reviewed a savings account and all will be able to compare the true cost of two loan offers. The six weekly sessions would cover income and spending, building a budget, saving, credit and loans, avoiding scams, and setting goals. Methods would be practical: budgeting with real prices from the local market, group games, a visit from a credit union officer and a mobile phone budgeting tool. Sessions would be held on Wednesday evenings at the community centre, as the needs survey suggests. Resources include a facilitator, two volunteers, printed workbooks in plain language, a projector, refreshments and a budget approved by the funder. Partners could include a credit union, a youth club and a church. Evaluation would use a short quiz in weeks one and six, a count of budgets completed, a follow-up call after three months and a short report to the funder.
markingPoints: States a clear aim and SMART objectives
Sets out sensible session content over six weeks
Chooses practical, participatory methods suited to young adults
Lists resources, partners, venue and timing
Plans evaluation with a baseline, follow-up and report

essays.stem: A dengue prevention project in St Thomas has a grant of J$450,000. Planned costs are: printing J$96,000; venue and chairs J$60,000; refreshments at J$200 per person per session for 100 people over six sessions; transport J$54,000; and a facilitator fee of J$15,000 per session for six sessions. Work out the total, compare it with the grant and recommend how the difference should be handled.
essays.modelAnswer: Refreshments cost J$200 × 100 people × 6 sessions = J$120,000. The facilitator costs J$15,000 × 6 = J$90,000. The total is J$96,000 + J$60,000 + J$120,000 + J$54,000 + J$90,000 = J$420,000. Checking another way: J$96,000 + J$60,000 = J$156,000; adding J$120,000 gives J$276,000; adding J$54,000 gives J$330,000; adding J$90,000 gives J$420,000. The grant is J$450,000, so J$30,000 is not yet allocated, about 6.7% of the grant. I would recommend keeping the J$30,000 as a contingency line, because prices for printing and transport may rise and a storm could force a session to be repeated. If it is still unspent near the end, I would ask the funder in writing whether it may be used for a follow-up yard check or a seventh session, since grant money should only be spent as agreed. I would track spending against each line monthly, keep receipts and report any variance in the final report.
markingPoints: Calculates refreshments J$120,000 and facilitator J$90,000
Calculates the total J$420,000 and checks it
Identifies J$30,000 (about 6.7%) left from the grant
Recommends a contingency and getting the funder's agreement before re-using it
Plans to track spending and report variances

essays.stem: Compare workshops, house-to-house visits and radio or social media as ways of delivering a community health education project, and recommend a mix for a rural community in upper Clarendon.
essays.modelAnswer: Workshops allow discussion, demonstrations and practice, so they are good for building skills and confidence, but they reach only people able to travel to the venue at the set time, and rural transport can be a barrier. House-to-house visits reach almost everyone, including the elderly and people with low literacy, and allow advice to fit each home, for example checking water drums, but they need many trained volunteers and much time. Radio and social media reach large numbers quickly and cheaply and repeat key messages, but they are one-way, cannot check understanding, and phone signal and data may be limited in hilly areas. For upper Clarendon, I would recommend a mix: two workshops held at the church hall after Sunday service and at the school on market day; house-to-house visits by trained peer educators to the most remote districts; and short messages on community radio and WhatsApp groups to remind people between visits. This combines skills, reach and repetition, and suits the area's distances and resources.
markingPoints: Gives strengths and limits of workshops
Gives strengths and limits of house-to-house visits
Gives strengths and limits of radio and social media
Recommends a clear mix for the rural setting
Justifies the mix by reach, skills, cost and local conditions

essays.stem: Explain how you would build and manage partnerships with a church, a school, the local health office and a local business for a community education project.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first work out what each partner can offer and what it wants. The church offers a trusted voice, a hall and volunteers; the school reaches children and parents; the health office gives accurate information and trained staff; a business may give money, goods or transport and wants goodwill. I would meet each partner, explain the needs evidence and the project's aims, and agree a role that suits it. Each arrangement would be written in a short letter of agreement or memorandum setting out roles, contributions, dates, use of logos, how money is handled and who speaks to the media. I would set up a small steering group with one person from each partner, meeting monthly to review progress. Communication would be regular and open, with quick updates by phone or WhatsApp. I would make sure no partner's interests, such as advertising or religious teaching, take over the project's neutral aim. Finally, I would thank and credit each partner publicly and share the evaluation, which builds trust for future projects.
markingPoints: Identifies what each partner offers and expects
Agrees roles in writing
Sets up joint coordination, such as a steering group
Keeps communication regular and protects the project's neutrality
Recognises partners and shares results

essays.stem: Explain how you would make a community education project accessible and inclusive for elderly residents, people with disabilities, people with low literacy and working parents.
essays.modelAnswer: For elderly residents, I would choose a venue that is close by, with step-free access, seats with backs, toilets and shade, and keep sessions short with breaks. Large print and clear speech would help those with poor sight or hearing. For people with disabilities, I would ask at registration what support they need, such as a ramp, a sign language interpreter, a helper or materials in another format, and arrange it in advance. For people with low literacy, I would use pictures, demonstrations and spoken explanation, read key points aloud, avoid written tests and use show-of-hands or picture cards for feedback, without drawing attention to anyone. For working parents, I would offer sessions at different times, including evenings or weekends, provide a supervised children's corner and share recordings or short summaries on WhatsApp. In every case, I would involve people from these groups in planning, test materials with them and ask for feedback. This makes sure the project reaches those who often miss out, not only those easiest to reach.
markingPoints: Gives suitable steps for elderly residents
Gives suitable steps for people with disabilities, asked in advance
Gives suitable steps for low literacy without embarrassment
Gives suitable steps for working parents (timing, childcare)
Involves these groups in planning and feedback

essays.stem: Describe how you would evaluate a community road safety education project for young motorcyclists, from the baseline to the final report.
essays.modelAnswer: At the planning stage, I would set objectives and indicators, for example the share of riders wearing helmets and the number of reported crashes involving young riders. Before the project starts, I would collect a baseline: helmet counts at three busy junctions on set days, a short survey of riders' knowledge and attitudes, and crash figures from the police or hospital where these can be shared. During the project, I would track attendance, the number of riders reached at bike stands and on social media, and feedback after each session, so that weak sessions can be improved. At the end, I would repeat the knowledge survey and the helmet counts on the same days of the week and at the same junctions, so the results are comparable. Three to six months later, I would count helmets again to see whether the change lasted. I would compare results with the baseline and the targets, consider other causes such as a police campaign, and write a final report with findings, costs, lessons learned and recommendations, shared with partners and the community.
markingPoints: Sets objectives and indicators at the planning stage
Collects a baseline before delivery
Monitors delivery and feedback during the project
Repeats measures fairly at the end and later, considering other causes
Reports results, costs and lessons to partners and the community

essays.stem: A youth reading project will use 12 volunteers working with children aged 8 to 12 on Saturdays. Explain how you would recruit, prepare, supervise and keep safe both the children and the volunteers.
essays.modelAnswer: I would recruit through churches, schools and youth clubs, with a short role description setting out the tasks, hours and expected behaviour. Each applicant would complete a form, give two references and have a police record check before working with children, in line with the organisation's safeguarding policy. Training would cover reading activities, managing behaviour positively, the code of conduct and what to do if a child discloses abuse: listen, do not promise secrecy and report to the named safeguarding lead at once. Volunteers would never be alone with a child out of sight; sessions would be held in an open hall, with at least two adults in each group. Parents would give written consent, contact details and information on health needs, and children would be signed in and out. I would supervise each Saturday, give feedback, hold a short debrief and keep a record of attendance and any incidents. To look after the volunteers, I would keep the workload reasonable, rotate tasks, thank them and listen to their concerns.
markingPoints: Recruits with a role description, references and police checks
Trains volunteers, including how to respond to disclosures
Sets safe working rules: no one alone with a child, open spaces, ratios
Gets parental consent and signs children in and out
Supervises, records incidents and supports volunteers

essays.stem: Halfway through a six-session project, attendance has fallen from 60 at the first session to 24 at the third, and the venue owner wants to raise the rent. Analyse the situation and recommend what you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: Attendance has fallen by 36 people, from 60 to 24, so only 40% of the first group still attend, a drop of 60%. This is serious, because the objectives depend on people completing the course, and the funder will judge the project on results. I would first find the causes by calling a sample of people who stopped coming and asking those still attending. Likely reasons include the time clashing with work or church, content that is too much like a lecture, transport costs or poor reminders. I would act on what I learn: change the time, make the sessions more practical, send WhatsApp reminders and ask community leaders to encourage people back. For the venue, I would check the agreement: if a price was agreed in writing for six sessions, I would politely hold the owner to it. If not, I would negotiate, perhaps offering credit in the project's publicity, or compare other venues such as a school or church hall, as long as moving does not confuse participants. I would inform the funder and the steering group of both issues and the actions taken.
markingPoints: Calculates the fall correctly (36 people; 40% remain, a 60% drop)
Explains why the drop matters for objectives and the funder
Finds the causes by asking those who left and those who stayed
Recommends practical actions to win people back
Handles the rent through the agreement, negotiation or alternatives, and informs the funder

essays.stem: Evaluate ways to make sure the benefits of a community education project continue after the funding ends, and explain what the final report to the funder should show.
essays.modelAnswer: One way is to train peer educators from the community, who can keep teaching neighbours. This is cheap and trusted, but needs ongoing support and recognition or people drift away. A second way is to hand the work to a lasting local body, such as a citizens' association, church or school club, with the materials and a simple plan. This gives a home for the work, but only if the body has the will and skills. A third way is to build the message into existing services, for example the health office's clinics or a school's curriculum, which lasts longest but needs agreement from those services. Leaving materials, a WhatsApp group and contacts with partners also helps. I would combine these, starting early rather than in the last week. The final report should show the objectives and how far each was met, with evidence compared with the baseline; the number reached and who was missed; spending against the budget with reasons for variances; problems and how they were handled; lessons learned; and the plan for continuing the work, with photos used only with consent.
markingPoints: Evaluates peer educators, with a strength and a limit
Evaluates handing over to a local body or existing services
Recommends combining methods and planning sustainability early
Report shows results against objectives and baseline, and reach
Report shows spending, problems, lessons and the continuation plan

practical1.title: Plan a community education project from a needs pack
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a needs pack for a made-up Jamaican community: a short profile (population, ages, reading levels, transport), survey results, notes from a focus group, a list of possible partners and a grant limit. The topic will be one of dengue prevention, hurricane preparedness, family budgeting or safe disposal of waste. As a group, prepare a project plan pack containing: a one-page needs summary; an aim and at least three SMART objectives; an outline of four to six sessions with learning outcomes and methods; a partner and promotion plan; a budget within the grant limit, with every sum checked twice; a risk and safeguarding plan; and an evaluation plan with a baseline. Finish with a one-page poster that sums up the plan for the community. Give each member a named role: project coordinator (keeps time, writes the aim and objectives and assembles the pack), needs analyst (writes the needs summary from the pack), session designer (plans the sessions and outcomes), budget officer (prepares and checks the budget), and evaluation and risk officer (writes the evaluation, risk and safeguarding plans). In a group of four, the coordinator also prepares the partner and promotion plan. At the end, each member explains their part to the assessor in two minutes.
materials: Needs pack and grant limit from the assessor
Computers with word-processing and spreadsheet software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes, markers and A3 paper for the poster
photos: The flipchart with roles, timetable and the key needs drawn from the pack
The session outline with learning outcomes and methods
The budget on screen or paper, with the second check marked
The risk, safeguarding and evaluation plans
The finished poster and the assembled plan pack
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the pack
Needs summary is drawn from the evidence in the pack, not guesswork
Objectives are SMART and match the needs found
Sessions and methods suit the community's ages, reading levels and timetable
Budget is within the grant, adds up correctly and was checked twice
Plan includes safeguarding, consent, access and a baseline for evaluation
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up community and data; do not name real residents
Keep the group's work in the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Listen to every member's ideas respectfully and share the work fairly
Take short breaks and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Prepare, deliver and evaluate a community education session
practical2.brief: Your group prepares and delivers a 30-minute community education session to other trainees, who play residents of a made-up community (the assessor gives each 'resident' a short role card, for example an elderly farmer, a young mother or a vendor with little time). The topic is agreed with the assessor, such as a family hurricane plan, keeping yards free of mosquito breeding sites, or a simple household budget. Before the session, make a picture-based handout or poster in plain language and a five-question quiz to use before and after. Deliver the session using at least one demonstration or hands-on activity, and handle questions. After it, mark the quizzes, work out the average before and after and the change in percentage points (checked twice), collect feedback with a show of hands or picture cards, and write a one-page evaluation with three improvements. Give each member a named role: lead facilitator (opens, links the parts and closes), activity leader (runs the demonstration or practice), materials designer (makes the handout or poster), evaluation officer (runs and marks the quiz and feedback), and reporter (writes the evaluation with the group). Every member must deliver part of the session. In a group of four, the reporter's role is shared by all.
materials: Topic agreed with the assessor, and 'resident' role cards
A3 paper, markers, coloured paper and a printer for the handout or poster
Props for the demonstration (for example an empty water drum and lid, a sample family plan, play money)
Quiz sheets, feedback cards and a calculator
photos: The session plan with times and who delivers each part
The handout or poster and the quiz
The session in progress, showing the demonstration or activity (work area only if anyone prefers no face)
Each member delivering their part (or their notes, if they prefer no photo)
The quiz results before and after, with the second check marked
The one-page evaluation with three improvements
checklist: Took a named role and delivered part of the session
Materials are accurate, plain and mostly pictures, suited to the 'residents'
Used a demonstration or activity that let 'residents' practise
Checked understanding and answered questions respectfully
Quiz averages and the change in percentage points are correct and were checked twice
Evaluation is honest and gives practical improvements
Kept to time and worked as part of the team
safety: Use only safe props: no real chemicals, sharp tools or medicines in the demonstration
Treat the 'residents' with respect and never make fun of a role card
Ask permission before photographing anyone; photograph materials and the work area if a person prefers
Keep the room tidy, cables taped down and walkways clear
